list.listitem: Consider myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) in patients with unexplained cytopenias, especially older patients or those who have undergone chemotherapy or radiotherapy for another disease. C
Bone marrow examination with cytogenetic studies is the most important diagnostic test. Without a bone marrow examination, there can never be diagnostic certainty about MDS. B

Patients with MDS who are potentially eligible for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation should be referred to an experienced transplant center for an opinion, since transplantation remains the only curative therapy for MDS. B

Azacitidine prolongs life in higher risk patients compared with standard of care; a survival study with decitabine is pending. Both drugs can reduce blast counts, improve blood counts, and induce cytogenetic remission, but at the risk of myelosuppression. B
Lenalidomide is effective for lower risk patients with a deletion of chromosome 5q. It is much less effective in patients without del(5q) and also causes a great deal of myelosuppression. B

Clinical trial enrollment remains important, as most patients will eventually die of complications of cytopenias or acute myeloid leukemia (AML) progression, and currently available drug therapies are inadequate. C

background.definition: The myelodysplastic syndromes include a diverse group of clonal disorders of hematopoietic progenitor cells. Key features include bone marrow failure, that is, an inability to produce normal numbers of healthy blood cells, and a risk of progression to acute myeloid leukemia.

list.listitem: Cancer registries have only recently begun to track MDS cases, so reliable epidemiologic numbers are not yet available.

The National Cancer Institute's SEER data from 2001 to 2003 suggested an overall incidence of 3.6 cases per 100,000 persons per year (males 4.9, females 2.9; 10,300 new cases per year in the United States). This is widely recognized as an underestimate.
The incidence of MDS increases dramatically with advancing age. For patients older than 80, studies in Europe have estimated the incidence at up to 40 cases per 100,000 persons per year.
Among patients older than 80, MDS is 3 times more common than acute leukemia.

In most cases, the cause of MDS is unknown. About 10% to 20% of patients have a history of exposure to ionizing radiation, alkylating agents (eg, melphalan, chlorambucil), or podophyllotoxins (eg, etoposide).

The bone marrow is usually hypercellular for age. Excessive intramedullary apoptosis (programmed cell death) causes the "MDS paradox" of low peripheral blood counts, despite increased marrow cellularity, at early stages of disease.

About 55% to 60% of patients have an abnormal karyotype, most commonly deletion of a whole chromosome or part of a chromosome. How these genomic changes contribute to MDS pathobiology is not yet known.
Some patients have an altered immune profile, including changes in various lymphocyte subsets and abnormal cytokine levels.
Epigenetic changes are common and include excessive cytosine methylation in gene promoter regions, which alters gene expression.

Iron metabolism is frequently disordered in MDS. About 10% to 15% of patients have abnormal ring sideroblasts in the marrow; these are erythroid precursors with iron-stuffed dysfunctional mitochondria surrounding the nucleus.

list.listitem: Suspect MDS in patients presenting with anemia (especially if the MCV is elevated or high normal) or other cytopenias without an obvious cause, particularly if the patient is older than 60 years or has received chemotherapy or radiation therapy. C
Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with cytogenetic testing is the most essential diagnostic assay for diagnosis of MDS and risk stratification of patients. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Low or borderline vitamin B12 levels, low folate levels
Thrombocytopenia and macrocytosis; other stigmata of alcoholism
HIV risk factors and positive HIV serology
Megakaryocyte clustering, heavy fibrosis, higher frequency of JAK2 V617F
LGL on peripheral smear and often positive T-cell gene rearrangement
Severely hypoplastic marrow; abnormal karyotype favors MDS
Ringed sideroblasts only without dysplasia in other lineages; often have ALAS2 mutations

list.listitem: In 2007, an international working group published a consensus statement for minimal diagnostic criteria for MDS. These include the following: Prerequisite criteria (both must be present): (1) presence of one or more peripheral blood cytopenias; and (2) exclusion of all other hematologic or nonhematologic disorders as a primary reason for the cytopenia. Decisive criteria (at least one must be present): (1) dysplasia in at least 10% of cells in one or more lineages (erythroid, neutrophilic, or megakaryocytic) or more than 15% ring sideroblasts on iron stain; (2) 5% to 19% blasts on bone marrow smears; or (3) typical chromosomal abnormality. Suggestive criteria (may provide supporting evidence but should not be used alone to make a diagnosis): (1) abnormal flow cytometry results indicated a monoclonal population of marrow cells; (2) other molecular evidence of a monoclonal cell population; (3) diminished ability of patient's blood and marrow to form progenitor cell colonies in vitro. Patients not meeting these criteria may be considered to have "idiopathic cytopenia of undetermined significance (ICUS)" and should be followed closely, as some will eventually develop MDS.
Fatigue is the most common symptom, reported by 89% of respondents in one global survey of 359 patients.

Easy bruising or bleeding is present in 55% of patients; most are thrombocytopenic, but some also have functional platelet defects. Up to 45% have pathologic night sweats. Other symptoms present in more than 20% of patients include: bone pain, fevers, dyspnea on exertion, recurrent infections (especially pneumonia, sinusitis, and cellulitis), and undesired weight loss.

Skin and conjunctival pallor and tachycardia are typical signs of anemia but are not specific for MDS. Oral purpura and skin petechiae often signify thrombocytopenia. Oral thrush or mucosal ulcers are common, especially in patients with neutropenia.
A wide variety of skin lesions may be present, especially in patients with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML).
Splenomegaly is uncommon (<10% of patients) and should prompt a search for another disorder.
At diagnosis, more than 85% of patients with MDS have anemia (macrocytic in 40%-60%), and 30% to 50% are neutropenic or thrombocytopenic.

Bone marrow aspirate is essential for quantifying the proportion of undifferentiated blasts and assessing cell morphology. Bone marrow biopsy is essential for estimating overall marrow cellularity and assessing architecture. Bone marrow cytogenetic studies are abnormal in 55% of cases and have prognostic value ().
Either genomic array or karyotyping can be used to identify cytogenetic abnormalities.
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) panel tests for MDS are offered by several reference laboratories but are not recommended unless karyotyping is unsuccessful.

Flow cytometry may be inaccurate due to processing artifact. However, flow cytometry provides supplemental information about cell surface markers that may allow lineage assignment. If strict protocols are followed, one expert panel recommends the use of flow cytometry immunophenotyping, although this may not be possible in all centers.

Initial evaluation should include a thorough history and physical examination, CBC with platelets and leukocyte differential, peripheral blood smear, and bone marrow aspiration and biopsy with iron stains and cytogenetic studies. Other important tests include serum erythropoietin level (if treatment with recombinant erythropoietin is contemplated), red cell folate and serum vitamin B12 levels, and serum ferritin.

In some cases, the following tests may be helpful: HLA typing, if the patient may be an allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant candidate; HIV testing, if HIV risk factors are present; reticulin staining of the marrow biopsy; FISH for platelet-derived growth factor receptor beta gene rearrangements, since patients who have these rearrangements may respond to imatinib treatment (but this test is only worth doing if patient has CMML); flow cytometry to evaluate for a PNH clone or LGL leukemia; and genetic evaluation and testing if the patient has a family history of cytopenias.
Supportive care with transfusions and antimicrobial drugs as indicated remains the mainstay of MDS therapy. B
Lenalidomide is the most appropriate treatment for lower risk patients with a deletion of chromosome 5q and is associated with transfusion independence and cytogenetic remissions. B

Iron chelation therapy is controversial and cannot be generally recommended. However, it may be reasonable to consider chelation therapy for patients with a good prognosis who are red cell transfusion dependent and have a ferritin level of more than 1000 ng/mL. C

For higher risk patients, decitabine or azacitidine are associated with complete hematologic and cytogenetic responses in 10% to 40% of patients; they also improve quality of life and may prolong life compared with supportive care alone. B
Offer allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation to suitable patients, especially if they have high-risk prognostic features such as a high marrow blast count. B
See National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines for specific recommendations for low and high risk MDS patients (free account required for healthcare providers).

Three drugs are FDA approved for MDS indications: azacitidine (approved in 2004), decitabine (2006), and the immunomodulatory drug lenalidomide (2005). A network meta-analysis comparing azacitidine with decitabine found no clear benefit of one agent or the other.
Azacitidine is the only agent that has been shown to improve survival in MDS compared with supportive care alone, from 15 months to 24 months (but only for higher risk patients).
Decitabine is associated with complete response rates of 30% to 40%; a randomized European study showed no survival benefit compared with supportive care.

Lenalidomide is most effective in lower risk anemic patients with deletions of chromosome 5q (67% transfusion independence rate and ~30% cytogenetic remission rate, with a median duration of response of >2 years). In patients without deletions of chromosome 5q, only 26% of patients achieve transfusion independence, with a median duration of response of 41 weeks.

The erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) epoetin alpha and darbepoetin alpha are associated with a 20% to 40% overall response rate (defined by improvement in hemoglobin of >1.5-2.0 g/dL in 8-12 weeks' time). ESAs should be reserved for patients with serum erythropoietin levels of less than 500 IU/mL. Medicare policy on reimbursement of ESA use is evolving.

For red cell transfusion-dependent patients with a serum ferritin level persistently greater than 1000 ng/mL who have low-risk MDS with a life expectancy of more than 3 years, consider iron chelation with deferasirox (oral) or deferoxamine (injectable). A Cochrane review found an absence of RCT evidence to support this approach, but there are ongoing trials that address use of this therapy.

A trial randomized 225 lower-risk myelodysplastic patients with serum ferritin >2247 pmol/L and prior receipt of 15 to 75 packed RBC units to deferasirox 10 to 40 mg/kg/day or placebo. The primary endpoint was time to non-fatal cardiac or hepatic event, conversion to acute myeloid leukemia, or death and was longer with deferasirox (median 3.9 vs 3.0 years, HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.42-0.96).

A study randomized 229 patients with lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes (2:1) to luspatercept or placebo. More patients in the luspatercept were transfusion independent for at least 8 weeks (38% vs 13%, p <0.001, NNT = 4).

A randomised comparison of luspatercept with erythropoietin-alfa in 356 low risk MDS patients demonstrated significant benefit in acheiving transfusion independence with luspatercept (59% versus 31% patients on epo, NNT = 4).

A further randomised trial in patients with lower risk MDS who had become refractory or resistant to ESAs tested imetelstat (a competitive telomerase inhibitor); 40% patients acheived transfusion independence for 8 weeks compared to 15% in control group (NNT = 4).

Younger patients (especially those <55 years) may be candidates for allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplanation (HCT), which remains the only curative therapy for MDS. Experience is growing in transplanting patients aged 55 to 70 using less intense conditioning approaches. Guidelines recommend that HCT be offered to all patients with advanced de novo myeloplastic syndrome. This includes patients with therapy related MDS, chromosomal abnormalities and mutations, and those with high-risk cytogenetic or molecular disease.
Leukemia-style induction therapy is toxic and requires prolonged hospitalization (>20 days). Remissions may be achieved in up to 60% to 70% of patients but generally are not durable.

A subset of patients with MDS, especially younger patients with lower risk disease, respond to treatment with antithymocyte globulin or other immunosuppressant drugs. The best way of predicting who will respond to this therapy is not known.
An RCT randomized 98 patients (median age 72 years) with low risk myelodysplastic syndrome to azacitidine or azacitidine plus epoetin-beta. There was no benefit to adding epoetin-beta.

Thrombocytopenia may respond to therapy with the thrombopoietin agonists romiplostim or eltrombopag, but progression to AML has been reported, which is sometimes reversible on discontinuation of the drug. However, a 5 year follow-up study found no difference in long-term risk of conversion to AML or death between groups.

Granulocyte/colony-stimulating factor ( filgrastim) may be reasonable to use if patients suffer recurrent pyogenic infections, but it does not improve survival in MDS. Pegfilgrastim is associated with leukemoid reactions and spontaneous splenic rupture and should be used with caution.
Urgent treatment of patients with febrile neutropenia with broad-spectrum antibiotics is essential.
If the patient may potentially be a hematopoietic stem cell transplant candidate, referral to a transplant center for an opinion is important.

Transfusion support (eg, red cells for symptomatic patients or those with a hemoglobin <8.0 g/dL, and platelets for symptomatic patients or those with a platelet count <10 x 109/L) remains a mainstay of MDS therapy.
Antibiotics as indicated for infections are also important, but there is no clear role for prophylactic antibiotics for neutropenic patients.

Adverse prognostic features include a high bone marrow blast count, 2 or 3 cytopenias rather than none or 1, and a poor-risk karyotype (ie, either a complex karyotype with 3 or more different abnormalities, or any abnormality of chromosome 7) (). B

The 1997 International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS) includes only a small number of karyotypes, but many other cytogenetic abnormalities have subsequently been shown to have prognostic value (). B
About two-thirds of patients with MDS will ultimately die of complications of the disease.

Overall, 25% of patients go on to develop AML. The others will die of infection (the number one cause of death in MDS), bleeding, complications of chronic anemia such as strokes and cardiac events, or unrelated causes (since most patients are elderly).

The most common infections in MDS are a consequence of neutropenia, neutrophil dysfunction, or both. These include: bacterial pneumonia (less commonly fungal lung infections, such as with Aspergillus organisms), sinusitis, bacteremia, cellulitis, neutropenic enterocolitis, bronchitis, otitis media, joint space infections, and others.

In addition to age and performance status, 3 factors predict patient survival and median time to AML progression: the bone marrow blast count (higher is worse), the number of cytopenias (having 2 or 3 is worse than none or 1), and the cytogenetic risk group. These 3 factors have been combined in the IPSS ().
The IPSS included only a small number of cytogenetic abnormalities. Additional abnormalities have subsequently been found to be of prognostic importance also ().

The frequency of CBC monitoring depends on the degree of cytopenias. For patients who require transfusion, weekly blood tests may be necessary. For patients with milder cytopenias, monthly blood tests may be more appropriate.

Measurement of serum ferritin is appropriate when the patient has received 20 to 25 U of blood, to assess the degree of iron overload (although elevated ferritin is not specific and can be raised in inflammatory conditions, etc., without true iron overload).
Advise patients to contact their doctors or go to an emergency department if they develop a fever while neutropenic.

Very frail patients, such as elderly patients with multiple comorbidities who reside in a nursing home, for whom the only viable therapy would be an ESA (ie, epoetin alpha or darbepoetin alpha) if a diagnosis of MDS were confirmed, may be spared a bone marrow examination. However, the diagnosis of MDS can never be entirely secure in such a setting, and other causes for cytopenias should be sought.
Childhood MDS is rare and is distinct from adult MDS in risk factors, outlook, and treatment.
